title: 2.7 Hyperparameter Tuning and Feature Importance
text:
11.1 Calculate SHAP values in R
XGBoost computes exact tree SHAP values natively. Passing predcontrib = TRUE returns one contribution per feature plus a BIAS column holding ϕ0\phi_0.

shap_matrix <- predict(
  tuned_xgb,
  validation_matrix,
  predcontrib = TRUE
)

dim(shap_matrix)

[1] 1644   12

colnames(shap_matrix)

 [1] "game_seconds_remaining" "home_score_diff"        "home_possession"       
 [4] "down1"                  "down2"                  "down3"                 
 [7] "down4"                  "ydstogo"                "yardline_100"          
[10] "home_timeouts"          "away_timeouts"          "BIAS"                  


The additivity property is not an approximation. For every state, the contributions and the bias sum exactly to the model’s raw log-odds output.

raw_scores <- predict(tuned_xgb, validation_matrix, outputmargin = TRUE)

tibble(
  max_absolute_difference = max(abs(rowSums(shap_matrix) - raw_scores))
)

# A tibble: 1 × 1
  max_absolute_difference
                    <dbl>
1              0.00000316



11.1.1 One local explanation
Take the state the model considers most favorable to the home team and read off which features produced that score.

most_confident <- which.max(raw_scores)

local_explanation <- tibble(
  feature = colnames(shap_matrix),
  contribution = as.numeric(shap_matrix[most_confident, ])
) %>%
  arrange(desc(abs(contribution)))

local_explanation

# A tibble: 12 × 2
   feature                contribution
   <chr>                         <dbl>
 1 home_score_diff             2.79   
 2 home_possession             0.339  
 3 BIAS                        0.261  
 4 yardline_100                0.176  
 5 game_seconds_remaining      0.152  
 6 home_timeouts               0.0613 
 7 ydstogo                    -0.0336 
 8 away_timeouts              -0.0157 
 9 down2                       0.00356
10 down4                      -0.00312
11 down1                       0      
12 down3                       0      

tibble(
  log_odds = raw_scores[most_confident],
  probability = 1 / (1 + exp(-raw_scores[most_confident])),
  home_score_diff = validation_data$home_score_diff[most_confident],
  minutes_remaining = round(validation_data$minutes_remaining[most_confident], 1),
  actual_home_win = validation_data$home_win[most_confident]
)

# A tibble: 1 × 5
  log_odds probability home_score_diff minutes_remaining actual_home_win
     <dbl>       <dbl>           <dbl>             <dbl>           <int>
1     3.73       0.976              19               3.5               1


A positive contribution pushed the log odds toward a home win and a negative one pushed them away. This is the direction that gain and impurity importance cannot supply.


11.1.2 Global summary and comparison with the other rankings

shap_importance <- tibble(
  feature = colnames(shap_matrix),
  mean_absolute_shap = colMeans(abs(shap_matrix))
) %>%
  filter(feature != "BIAS") %>%
  arrange(desc(mean_absolute_shap))

ggplot(
  shap_importance,
  aes(x = mean_absolute_shap, y = reorder(feature, mean_absolute_shap))
) +
  geom_col(fill = "#276FBF") +
  labs(
    title = "Global SHAP importance",
    subtitle = "Mean absolute contribution to the log-odds prediction",
    x = "Mean |SHAP value|",
    y = NULL
  ) +
  theme_minimal()








Compare the three rankings this tutorial has now produced for the same problem.

rank_of <- function(data, feature_column, value_column) {
  data %>%
    arrange(desc(.data[[value_column]])) %>%
    transmute(
      feature = .data[[feature_column]],
      rank = row_number()
    )
}

rank_of(impurity_importance, "feature", "impurity") %>%
  rename(impurity_rank = rank) %>%
  full_join(
    rank_of(permutation_importance, "feature", "importance") %>%
      rename(permutation_rank = rank),
    by = "feature"
  ) %>%
  full_join(
    rank_of(shap_importance, "feature", "mean_absolute_shap") %>%
      rename(shap_rank = rank),
    by = "feature"
  ) %>%
  arrange(impurity_rank)

# A tibble: 12 × 4
   feature                impurity_rank permutation_rank shap_rank
   <chr>                          <int>            <int>     <int>
 1 home_score_diff                    1                1         1
 2 game_seconds_remaining             2                2         3
 3 yardline_100                       3                4         4
 4 ydstogo                            4                8         8
 5 home_possession                    5                3         2
 6 down                               6                6        NA
 7 away_timeouts                      7                5         7
 8 home_timeouts                      8                7         5
 9 down4                             NA               NA         6
10 down2                             NA               NA         9
11 down1                             NA               NA        10
12 down3                             NA               NA        11


The three columns do not agree, and they are not supposed to. Impurity is a training-data property of a random forest, permutation is a validation-loss property of that same forest, and SHAP is a structural property of the boosted model. Note also that SHAP is computed on the dummy-coded matrix, so the factor down appears as separate indicator columns rather than one variable. Report the definition, the model, and the data set alongside any ranking.

2 Three related implementations
XGBoost, LightGBM, and CatBoost all construct additive ensembles of trees. They differ in how they search for splits, grow trees, handle categories, and control overfitting.








Implementation
Distinctive idea
Especially useful when




XGBoost
Regularized second-order boosting
You want a mature, flexible general-purpose baseline


LightGBM
Histogram splits and leaf-wise growth
Data are large and training speed matters


CatBoost
Ordered boosting and native categorical handling
The data contain important categorical variables



These are tendencies, not guarantees. The best choice depends on validation performance, computation, interpretability, and maintenance requirements.

title: 2.5 LightGBM and CatBoost
text:
3 LightGBM intuition
Instead of evaluating every observed numeric value as a potential split, LightGBM groups values into histogram bins. This can substantially reduce the work needed to evaluate splits.
LightGBM also commonly grows a tree leaf-wise: it splits the current leaf with the largest estimated improvement. A leaf-wise tree can reduce loss quickly, but it can overfit small data if controls such as num_leaves, max_depth, and min_data_in_leaf are too permissive.
Suppose two candidate leaves would reduce the loss by 0.12 and 0.04. A leaf-wise procedure chooses the 0.12 leaf next. A level-wise procedure might split both leaves at the same depth, even though one offers much less improvement.

text:
4 Fit LightGBM

analysis_matrix <- model_matrix(analysis_data)
validation_matrix <- model_matrix(validation_data)

lgb_analysis <- lgb.Dataset(
  data = analysis_matrix,
  label = analysis_data$home_win
)
lgb_validation <- lgb.Dataset.create.valid(
  dataset = lgb_analysis,
  data = validation_matrix,
  label = validation_data$home_win
)

lgb_parameters <- list(
  objective = "binary",
  metric = "binary_logloss",
  learning_rate = 0.05,
  num_leaves = 15,
  max_depth = 5,
  min_data_in_leaf = 50,
  feature_fraction = 0.80,
  bagging_fraction = 0.80,
  bagging_freq = 1,
  lambda_l2 = 1,
  seed = 431,
  verbosity = -1
)

lgb_fit <- lgb.train(
  params = lgb_parameters,
  data = lgb_analysis,
  nrounds = 500,
  valids = list(validation = lgb_validation),
  early_stopping_rounds = 30,
  verbose = -1
)

lgb_probability <- predict(lgb_fit, validation_matrix)
probability_metrics(
  validation_data$home_win,
  lgb_probability,
  "LightGBM"
)

title: 2.5 LightGBM and CatBoost
text:
5 CatBoost intuition
Team, formation, venue, and play type are categorical variables. Converting a category to its overall outcome average can leak the target into its own feature. CatBoost combats this with ordered target statistics: for each training row, the encoded value is constructed using earlier rows in a random ordering rather than the row’s own outcome.
For example, suppose the earlier home-team outcomes in an ordering are (1,0,1). With a prior mean of 0.50 and prior weight 2, a smoothed category statistic is
1+0+1+2(0.50)3+2=0.60.
\frac{1+0+1 + 2(0.50)}{3+2}=0.60.

The current row’s outcome is not used in its own encoding. CatBoost also uses ordered boosting to reduce another form of prediction shift created when the same observations define residuals and fit the next tree.

title: 2.5 LightGBM and CatBoost
text:
6 Fit CatBoost with native categories
This example adds play type to the common game-state predictors. CatBoost receives factor columns directly. Team identifiers were considered but rejected because they worsened game-grouped validation log loss; including a categorical variable is not automatically beneficial.

catboost_features <- c(
  wp_predictors,
  "play_type"
)

analysis_cat <- analysis_data %>%
  select(all_of(catboost_features)) %>%
  mutate(across(where(is.character), as.factor))

validation_cat <- validation_data %>%
  select(all_of(catboost_features)) %>%
  mutate(across(where(is.character), as.factor))

cat_analysis <- catboost.load_pool(
  data = analysis_cat,
  label = analysis_data$home_win
)
cat_validation <- catboost.load_pool(
  data = validation_cat,
  label = validation_data$home_win
)

cat_parameters <- list(
  loss_function = "Logloss",
  eval_metric = "Logloss",
  iterations = 400,
  depth = 4,
  learning_rate = 0.03,
  l2_leaf_reg = 10,
  random_seed = 431,
  od_type = "Iter",
  od_wait = 30,
  logging_level = "Silent"
)

cat_fit <- catboost.train(
  learn_pool = cat_analysis,
  test_pool = cat_validation,
  params = cat_parameters
)

cat_probability <- catboost.predict(
  cat_fit,
  cat_validation,
  prediction_type = "Probability"
)

probability_metrics(
  validation_data$home_win,
  cat_probability,
  "CatBoost"
)

# A tibble: 1 × 4
  model    brier log_loss accuracy
  <chr>    <dbl>    <dbl>    <dbl>
1 CatBoost 0.187    0.546    0.712

text:
8 What should be tuned?








Model
High-impact parameters
Important interaction




LightGBM
learning_rate, num_leaves, min_data_in_leaf, feature_fraction, bagging_fraction
Large num_leaves usually requires a larger min_data_in_leaf


CatBoost
learning_rate, depth, l2_leaf_reg, random_strength, bagging_temperature
Smaller learning rates normally require more iterations



For both implementations, begin with a deliberately large iteration limit and let early stopping choose the effective number of trees. Then tune structural and sampling parameters with the same grouped game splits. Tuning iterations independently of learning_rate is inefficient because they jointly determine how far the ensemble can move.
LightGBM’s leaf-wise growth makes num_leaves especially important. A depth limit of dd permits at most 2d2^d leaves in a complete binary tree, but a leaf-wise tree need not be balanced. Consequently, num_leaves should generally be substantially smaller than 2𝚖𝚊𝚡_𝚍𝚎𝚙𝚝𝚑2^{\texttt{max\_depth}} when both controls are active.
CatBoost’s default symmetric trees apply the same split condition to all nodes at a given depth. A depth-dd symmetric tree has up to 2d2^d leaves, so increasing depth can increase the number of leaf values exponentially.

title: 2.5 LightGBM and CatBoost
section: 9 How their built-in importance scores differ
text:
9 How their built-in importance scores differ
LightGBM commonly reports:

gain importance: the sum of training-objective reductions from splits using a feature; and
split importance: the number of retained splits using the feature.

Gain and split count need not rank features the same way. One feature may create a few large improvements, while another appears in many small refinements.
For non-ranking CatBoost models, the default PredictionValuesChange importance measures how much model predictions change, on average, across pairs of leaves whose paths differ because of a feature. Leaf observation weights are used when aggregating those changes. LossFunctionChange instead approximates how much a selected evaluation loss worsens when the feature is removed from the model’s calculations. It requires evaluation data and can be negative.
None of these definitions supplies an effect direction or a causal conclusion. Tutorial 2.7 compares them with validation-set permutation importance calculated using the same log-loss scale for every model.

10 Practice questions

Why can histogram-based splitting make LightGBM faster?
What is the main overfitting risk of aggressive leaf-wise growth?
Why should a row’s outcome not be used to construct its own target-encoded feature?
If the data contain only eight clean numeric game-state variables, which CatBoost advantage is less relevant?
Why is it inappropriate to choose the number of boosting rounds using the 2023 test season?







TipShow answers






The algorithm evaluates a smaller set of binned candidate cut points instead of every distinct numeric value.
It can repeatedly grow a small, highly specific region and fit noise. Limits on leaves, depth, and minimum leaf size help.
That would leak target information and make training performance look unrealistically strong.
Its native treatment of categorical variables is less relevant, although its boosting and tree construction may still perform well.
The test season is intended to estimate performance on unseen future data. Using it for model selection makes that estimate optimistic.

title: 2.5 LightGBM and CatBoost
text:
11 Key takeaways

XGBoost, LightGBM, and CatBoost build the same kind of additive ensemble and differ in how they search, grow, and encode.
Histogram binning and leaf-wise growth make LightGBM fast but make num_leaves the critical control.
Ordered target statistics let CatBoost encode categories without leaking a row’s own outcome into its own feature.
Hold the split, target, information set, metric, and tuning budget constant when comparing implementations.
Each library defines importance differently, so always report which definition and which data set produced a ranking.

title: 2.3 Bagging and Random Forests
section: 4.1 Vote share is not a probability
text:
4.1 Vote share is not a probability
predict() on a bagged classifier can return two very different quantities, and the difference matters more than any tuning parameter in this tutorial.

aggregation = "majority", the ipred default, returns the fraction of trees that voted for each class. When every tree agrees, the reported value is exactly 0 or 1.
aggregation = "average" averages the trees’ leaf probabilities. This is the ensemble probability p̂bag(x)\hat p_{bag}(x) defined above.


bagged_votes <- predict(
  bagged_fit,
  newdata = validation_data,
  type = "prob",
  aggregation = "majority"
)[, "win"]

bagged_probability <- predict(
  bagged_fit,
  newdata = validation_data,
  type = "prob",
  aggregation = "average"
)[, "win"]

tibble(
  aggregation = c("majority (vote share)", "average (leaf probabilities)"),
  exactly_0_or_1 = c(
    mean(bagged_votes %in% c(0, 1)),
    mean(bagged_probability %in% c(0, 1))
  ),
  distinct_values = c(
    dplyr::n_distinct(bagged_votes),
    dplyr::n_distinct(bagged_probability)
  )
)

# A tibble: 2 × 3
  aggregation                  exactly_0_or_1 distinct_values
  <chr>                                 <dbl>           <int>
1 majority (vote share)                 0.195              76
2 average (leaf probabilities)          0                1315


A unanimous vote is not certainty; it only means the bootstrap trees agreed. A 0 or 1 report is a claim that the outcome is impossible, and log loss treats it as such. Compare the two on the same games.

bind_rows(
  probability_metrics(
    validation_data$home_win,
    bagged_votes,
    model = "Bagged trees (majority vote share)"
  ),
  probability_metrics(
    validation_data$home_win,
    bagged_probability,
    model = "Bagged trees (averaged probabilities)"
  )
)

# A tibble: 2 × 4
  model                                 brier log_loss accuracy
  <chr>                                 <dbl>    <dbl>    <dbl>
1 Bagged trees (majority vote share)    0.203    0.735    0.690
2 Bagged trees (averaged probabilities) 0.189    0.554    0.695


The Brier scores are similar because squared error is bounded. Log loss is not bounded, so the unanimous states dominate it. Always confirm which quantity a classification package returns before treating its output as a probability.






Tip



This is one reason the course uses ranger rather than randomForest for forests. Setting probability = TRUE builds a probability forest, which averages the trees’ leaf probabilities rather than counting their votes. randomForest::predict(type = "prob") reports vote shares and offers no averaging option at all.

title: 2.1 NFL Win Probability and a Logistic Baseline
text:
9.1 What calibration means
A model is calibrated when states assigned probability 0.70 lead to home wins approximately 70% of the time. Formally, writing p̂(X)\hat p(X) for the model’s forecast, calibration is the requirement
P{Y=1∣p̂(X)=p}=pfor every p∈[0,1].
P\{Y=1\mid \hat p(X)=p\}=p
\qquad\text{for every } p\in[0,1].

Read that carefully: it conditions on what the model said. It asks whether the number the model produces means what it claims to mean. That is a different question from either of the two you have already met.






ImportantWhy calibration matters more here than in most classification problems



In most applications a probability is an intermediate quantity and only the final label is used. In win probability the number is the product. It is printed on a broadcast graphic, drives a fourth-down decision model, sizes a position, and is quoted back at the analyst on Monday. A model that says 90% when the truth is 70% is wrong in a way no downstream threshold can repair.

title: 2.1 NFL Win Probability and a Logistic Baseline
text:
9.2 Read the plot
Each point is a bin of states with similar predictions. The horizontal position is the average forecast in that bin; the vertical position is the fraction that actually ended in a home win. Perfect calibration puts every point on the 45-degree line.

A point below the line means the model promised more than it delivered: overconfident in that range.
A point above the line means the outcome happened more often than predicted: underconfident.
A curve that is systematically flatter than the diagonal — high predictions too high and low predictions too low — is the classic signature of an overconfident model, and it is the pattern recalibration can repair.

Point size matters as much as position. A bin holding twenty states will bounce around the line from sampling noise alone, so read the large bins first and treat small ones as suggestive. Tutorial 2.6 quantifies this and shows how to fix a miscalibrated model.

logistic_calibration <- calibration_table(
  validation_data$home_win,
  validation_probability
)

ggplot(
  logistic_calibration,
  aes(x = mean_prediction, y = observed_win_rate, size = states)
) +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_point(color = "#1f77b4", alpha = 0.8) +
  coord_equal(xlim = c(0, 1), ylim = c(0, 1)) +
  labs(
    title = "Logistic baseline calibration",
    x = "Mean predicted home-win probability",
    y = "Observed home-win rate",
    size = "States"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

title: NFL In-Game Win Probability with Tree-Based Models
text:
1 Overview
This sequence develops an NFL in-game win-probability model from a logistic-regression baseline through modern tree ensembles. One modeling problem, one data definition, and one evaluation design are used throughout so that differences in performance can be attributed to the models rather than to changing data pipelines.
The central prediction is
P(home team eventually wins∣current game state).
P(\text{home team eventually wins}\mid\text{current game state}).

The response equals 1 when the home team eventually wins and 0 otherwise. Every predictor must be known at the moment of prediction.


2 Tutorial map








Tutorial

Models




2.1

2.2

2.4

2.7

3 Data
The local file data/nfl_wp_states.rds is generated from 2022 and 2023 regular-season play-by-play data distributed through nflreadr. To keep classroom computation manageable, the preparation script retains one eligible state per game per two-minute block of regulation.

library(dplyr)

nfl_states <- readRDS("data/nfl_wp_states.rds")

nfl_states %>%
  summarize(
    states = n(),
    games = n_distinct(game_id),
    seasons = paste(sort(unique(season)), collapse = ", "),
    home_win_rate = mean(home_win)
  )

1  16581   541 2022, 2023         0.558








Note



This is a teaching sample, not a production win-probability data set. A production system should retain every eligible state, document data latency, address overtime explicitly, and monitor rule and strategy changes across seasons.




4 Reproducibility files

R/prepare_nfl_wp_data.R downloads and prepares the teaching data.
R/modeling_helpers.R defines the common split and probability metrics.
R/build_model_comparison.R creates the final held-out prediction file.
data/README.md records provenance and filtering decisions.



5 Required packages

install.packages(c(
  "dplyr",
  "ggplot2",
  "nflreadr",
  "rpart",
  "rpart.plot",
  "ipred",
  "ranger",
  "xgboost",
  "lightgbm"
))

CatBoost distributes released R binaries through GitHub rather than CRAN. Follow the current official CatBoost R installation instructions before Tutorial 2.5.


6 Modeling rules used throughout

Use 2022 for model development and leave 2023 untouched until final evaluation.
Assign all states from the same game to the same resample.
Fit preprocessing steps using training data only.
Use Brier score and log loss as primary metrics.
Examine calibration, not only ranking or classification accuracy.
Compare every complex model with the logistic baseline.

title: 2.2 Classification and Regression Trees (CART)
text:
1 Learning objectives
After completing this tutorial, you should be able to:

calculate classification impurity and regression squared error;
explain greedy recursive partitioning;
distinguish classification-tree and regression-tree predictions;
derive the score used to select a split;
use cost-complexity pruning and tuning parameters to control overfitting; and
fit and evaluate CART models in R.



2 The CART idea
A decision tree repeatedly divides the predictor space into regions. Within each terminal region, the model makes one constant prediction.

Every internal node asks one yes/no question about a single predictor. Every path from the root down to a leaf is a chain of those questions joined by “and”, and the leaf at the end of that path is one region RmR_m. A tree with MM leaves therefore writes its prediction as
f̂(x)=∑m=1Mcm𝟏(x∈Rm),
\hat f(x)=\sum_{m=1}^{M}c_m\,\mathbf 1(x\in R_m),

where exactly one indicator is ever equal to one. In the diagram above,
R1={home_score_diff<0}∩{minutes_remaining<10},
R_1=\{\text{home\_score\_diff}<0\}\cap\{\text{minutes\_remaining}<10\},

and a state falling in R1R_1 receives the prediction c1c_1 no matter where inside R1R_1 it sits. The regions do not overlap and together they cover the whole predictor space.
For classification, a leaf predicts class probabilities. For regression, a leaf predicts the mean response. The tree is interpretable because every prediction follows a sequence of if/then rules.


3 Impurity for classification trees
For node RR with class proportions p1R,…,pKRp_{1R},\ldots,p_{KR}, Gini impurity is
G(R)=1−∑k=1KpkR2.
G(R)=1-\sum_{k=1}^{K}p_{kR}^2.

For a binary outcome with home-win proportion pRp_R,
G(R)=2pR(1−pR).
G(R)=2p_R(1-p_R).

Entropy is an alternative:
H(R)=−∑k=1KpkRlog⁡(pkR).
H(R)=-\sum_{k=1}^{K}p_{kR}\log(p_{kR}).

A candidate split ss divides a parent node RR into children RleftR_{\mathrm{left}} and RrightR_{\mathrm{right}}. Its improvement is
ΔI(s,R)=I(R)−nleftnI(Rleft)−nrightnI(Rright),
\Delta I(s,R)
=I(R)-\frac{n_{\mathrm{left}}}{n}I(R_{\mathrm{left}})
-\frac{n_{\mathrm{right}}}{n}I(R_{\mathrm{right}}),

where nn is the number of observations in the parent node, and nleftn_{\mathrm{left}} and nrightn_{\mathrm{right}} are the numbers in the left and right children.
At a node, CART evaluates the allowable variable-threshold pairs and chooses
s*=arg⁡maxsΔI(s,R).
s^*=\arg\max_s \Delta I(s,R).

This is a greedy choice: CART selects the best split now without searching over all possible future trees. The greedy strategy is computationally practical, but it does not guarantee the globally optimal tree.


4 Numerical classification example
Consider six game states:

hand_example <- tibble(
  state = 1:6,
  home_score_diff = c(10, 7, 3, 1, -4, -8),
  seconds_remaining = c(300, 480, 120, 900, 600, 300),
  home_possession = c(1, 0, 1, 0, 1, 0),
  home_win = c(1, 1, 1, 0, 0, 0)
)

For the split home_score_diff > 0:

the positive node has three wins in four states, so Gleft=2(.75)(.25)=.375G_{\mathrm{left}}=2(.75)(.25)=.375;
the nonpositive node has zero wins in two states, so Gright=0G_{\mathrm{right}}=0; and

gini <- function(y) {
  p <- mean(y)
  2 * p * (1 - p)
}

root_gini <- gini(hand_example$home_win)

The estimated leaf probabilities are .75 and 0. The second value is implausibly confident because the node contains only two observations. Minimum node sizes, pruning, and calibration help address this problem.


5 How recursive partitioning builds a tree
Starting with all training observations in the root node, CART repeats the following operations:

Generate candidate splits for every eligible predictor.
Calculate ΔI(s,R)\Delta I(s,R) for every candidate.
Select the candidate with the largest reduction in impurity.
Send observations to the two child nodes.
Repeat within each child until a stopping rule is reached.

For a binary classification leaf RR, the raw probability estimate is
p̂R=1nR∑i:xi∈Ryi.
\hat p_R=\frac{1}{n_R}\sum_{i:x_i\in R}y_i.

An optional Laplace-smoothed estimate is
p̃R=n1R+anR+2a,
\tilde p_R=\frac{n_{1R}+a}{n_R+2a},

where n1Rn_{1R} is the number of wins and a>0a>0 is a smoothing constant. With two losses and a=1a=1, the raw estimate is 0 but the smoothed estimate is 1/(2+2)=.251/(2+2)=.25. The rpart probabilities shown in this tutorial are the raw leaf proportions; the smoothing formula explains one way to reduce extreme estimates in small leaves.


6 Regression trees
For a continuous response, a node predicts its mean:
ŷR=1nR∑i:xi∈Ryi.
\hat y_R=\frac{1}{n_R}\sum_{i:x_i\in R}y_i.

CART chooses the split that produces the largest reduction in squared error:
SSE(R)=∑i:xi∈R(yi−y‾R)2.
SSE(R)=\sum_{i:x_i\in R}(y_i-\bar y_R)^2.


regression_example <- hand_example %>%
  mutate(final_margin = c(12, 8, 5, -2, -6, -10))

root_sse <- sum(
  (regression_example$final_margin - mean(regression_example$final_margin))^2
)

  mutate(node = home_score_diff > 0) %>%
  group_by(node) %>%
  summarize(
    node_sse = sum((final_margin - mean(final_margin))^2),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  summarize(total = sum(node_sse)) %>%
  pull(total)

8 Cost-complexity pruning
For tree TT, cost-complexity pruning minimizes
Rα(T)=R(T)+α|T|,
R_\alpha(T)=R(T)+\alpha|T|,

where R(T)R(T) is training loss, |T||T| is the number of terminal nodes, and α\alpha penalizes complexity.
For any fixed α\alpha, a larger tree is retained only when its reduction in training loss is large enough to pay the penalty for its additional leaves. Increasing α\alpha therefore produces a nested sequence of smaller subtrees.
rpart reports its own cross-validated error in the xerror column, and it is tempting to prune at cp with the smallest xerror. Do not do that here. rpart cross-validates by splitting rows at random, which is exactly the leakage Tutorial 2.1 warns against: states from one game land in both the training and held-out folds, and the resulting xerror is optimistic.
Select the complexity on whole validation games instead.

candidate_cp <- unique(classification_tree$cptable[, "CP"])

cp_search <- lapply(candidate_cp, function(cp_value) {
  candidate_probability <- predict(
    prune(classification_tree, cp = cp_value),
    newdata = validation_data,
    type = "prob"
  )[, "win"]

  tibble(
    cp = cp_value,
    leaves = sum(
      prune(classification_tree, cp = cp_value)$frame$var == "<leaf>"
    ),
    log_loss = log_loss(validation_data$home_win, candidate_probability)
  )
}) %>%

12 Strengths and limitations
Single trees are easy to explain and automatically represent nonlinear relationships and interactions. They are also unstable: a small change in data can alter the first split and much of the remaining tree. Their piecewise-constant probabilities are often poorly calibrated. Ensembles address stability and predictive accuracy at the cost of simplicity.

    home_possession + down + ydstogo + yardline_100 +
    home_timeouts + away_timeouts,
  data = analysis_data,
  method = "class",
  control = rpart.control(cp = 0, minsplit = 100, maxdepth = 3)

brier_score(validation_data$home_win, shallow_probability)

4. Larger leaves generally reduce variance and increase bias. Predictions become more stable and less extreme, but the tree may miss real local structure.





14 Key takeaways

Classification trees minimize impurity; regression trees minimize squared error.
Trees discover thresholds and interactions automatically.
Unrestricted growth overfits, so pruning and node-size controls matter.
A single tree is an explanatory starting point, not usually the strongest probability model.

text:
2 Boosting versus bagging
Bagging fits many trees independently and averages them. Boosting fits trees sequentially. Each new tree is chosen to improve the current ensemble where it is still making mistakes.
For MM trees, a gradient boosted model has the additive form
FM(x)=F0(x)+η∑m=1Mfm(x),
F_M(x) = F_0(x) + \eta\sum_{m=1}^{M} f_m(x),

where fm(x)f_m(x) is tree mm and 0<η≤10 < \eta \leq 1 is the learning rate. For binary outcomes, the score is converted to a probability with
p̂(x)=11+exp⁡[−FM(x)].
\hat p(x)=\frac{1}{1+\exp[-F_M(x)]}.

A smaller learning rate makes each tree’s contribution more cautious. It normally requires more trees, but it often improves generalization.

title: 2.4 Gradient Boosting and XGBoost
text:
3 Gradient boosting as stagewise optimization
Let L(y,F(x))L(y,F(x)) be a differentiable loss. The ideal prediction function minimizes empirical risk:
F̂=arg⁡minF∑i=1nL{yi,F(xi)}.
\hat F=\arg\min_F\sum_{i=1}^{n}L\{y_i,F(x_i)\}.

Boosting searches for FF stage by stage rather than optimizing over every possible tree ensemble at once.
First, initialize the model with the best constant:
F0(x)=arg⁡minc∑i=1nL(yi,c).
F_0(x)=\arg\min_c\sum_{i=1}^{n}L(y_i,c).

At round mm, calculate each observation’s negative gradient, or pseudo-residual:
rim=−∂L(yi,F(xi))∂F(xi)|F=Fm−1.
r_{im}=-\left.
\frac{\partial L(y_i,F(x_i))}{\partial F(x_i)}
\right|_{F=F_{m-1}}.

Fit a regression tree to rimr_{im}. If that tree has terminal regions R1m,…,RJmR_{1m},\ldots,R_{Jm}, choose the update in each region by
γjm=arg⁡minγ∑xi∈RjmL{yi,Fm−1(xi)+γ}.
\gamma_{jm}=\arg\min_\gamma
\sum_{x_i\in R_{jm}}
L\{y_i,F_{m-1}(x_i)+\gamma\}.

Finally update
Fm(x)=Fm−1(x)+η∑j=1Jγjm𝟏(x∈Rjm).
F_m(x)=F_{m-1}(x)
+\eta\sum_{j=1}^{J}\gamma_{jm}\mathbf 1(x\in R_{jm}).

The tree determines where the model changes; γjm\gamma_{jm} determines how far it changes; and η\eta shrinks that change.

text:
4 A one-step numerical example
Suppose the current model gives three game states probabilities (0.50,0.50,0.50)(0.50, 0.50, 0.50), while the outcomes are y=(1,0,1)y=(1,0,1). For logistic loss, the negative gradient is
ri=yi−p̂i.
r_i = y_i - \hat p_i.

The pseudo-residuals are therefore (0.50,−0.50,0.50)(0.50,-0.50,0.50). Imagine a small tree groups states 1 and 3 in one leaf and state 2 in another. If the leaf updates are +0.50+0.50 and −0.50-0.50, and the learning rate is η=0.20\eta=0.20, the new scores are
F1=(0.10,−0.10,0.10).
F_1=(0.10,-0.10,0.10).

The probabilities become approximately (0.525,0.475,0.525)(0.525,0.475,0.525). One weak tree has moved every prediction in the correct direction. Later trees repeat this process.

title: 2.4 Gradient Boosting and XGBoost
text:
5 What XGBoost adds
XGBoost uses a second-order approximation to the loss. At boosting step tt, it minimizes approximately
∑i[gift(xi)+12hift(xi)2]+Ω(ft),
\sum_i \left[g_i f_t(x_i) + \frac{1}{2}h_i f_t(x_i)^2\right]
+ \Omega(f_t),

where gig_i and hih_i are the first and second derivatives of the loss and Ω\Omega penalizes tree complexity. For logistic loss,
gi=p̂i−yi,hi=p̂i(1−p̂i).
g_i=\hat p_i-y_i, \qquad h_i=\hat p_i(1-\hat p_i).

If a leaf contains observations II, define G=∑i∈IgiG=\sum_{i\in I}g_i and H=∑i∈IhiH=\sum_{i\in I}h_i. With an L2 penalty λ\lambda, the optimal leaf weight is
w*=−GH+λ.
w^*=-\frac{G}{H+\lambda}.

This formula makes the intuition concrete: a leaf receives a large update when its combined error GG is large, but the Hessian and regularization shrink unstable updates.
For a candidate split into left and right children, define (GL,HL)(G_L,H_L) and (GR,HR)(G_R,H_R) as their gradient and Hessian sums. XGBoost’s regularized split improvement is
Gain⁡=12[GL2HL+λ+GR2HR+λ−(GL+GR)2HL+HR+λ]−γ,
\operatorname{Gain}
=\frac{1}{2}\left[
\frac{G_L^2}{H_L+\lambda}
+\frac{G_R^2}{H_R+\lambda}
-\frac{(G_L+G_R)^2}{H_L+H_R+\lambda}
\right]-\gamma,

where γ\gamma is the penalty for creating another leaf. The split is retained only when its gain is positive and any minimum-child constraints are satisfied.

5.1 Numerical split-gain example
Suppose GL=−3G_L=-3, HL=2H_L=2, GR=2G_R=2, HR=3H_R=3, λ=1\lambda=1, and γ=0\gamma=0. Then
Gain⁡=12[93+44−16]=1.917.
\operatorname{Gain}
=\frac{1}{2}\left[
\frac{9}{3}+\frac{4}{4}-\frac{1}{6}
\right]
=1.917.

If γ=2\gamma=2, the regularized gain becomes −0.083-0.083, so XGBoost rejects the split. This example shows that gamma is expressed on the objective-improvement scale rather than as a tree depth or sample count.

7 How XGBoost feature importance is calculated
For every retained split, XGBoost records its regularized objective improvement. For feature jj, raw total gain is
Gj=∑s:v(s)=jGain⁡s.
G_j=\sum_{s:v(s)=j}\operatorname{Gain}_s.

The reported Gain column normalizes these totals:
ImportanceGain⁡j=Gj∑kGk.
\operatorname{ImportanceGain}_j
=\frac{G_j}{\sum_k G_k}.

Thus, a value of .40 means that splits using that feature account for 40% of the summed training-objective improvement across the fitted trees. Frequency is the fraction of retained splits using the feature. Cover summarizes the amount of training information affected by those splits; for second-order boosting it is based on Hessian mass rather than only the number of rows.
Gain describes how the fitted model used a feature. It does not show the direction of an effect, does not establish causality, and can divide importance unpredictably among correlated predictors.

importance <- xgb.importance(
  feature_names = colnames(analysis_matrix),
  model = xgb_fit
) %>%
  slice_head(n = 10)

ggplot(importance, aes(x = Gain, y = reorder(Feature, Gain))) +
  geom_col(fill = "#276FBF") +
  labs(
    title = "XGBoost feature importance",
    x = "Share of total gain",
    y = NULL
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

8 Regularization controls








Parameter
What it controls
Typical effect of increasing it




eta
Size of each boosting step
Slower, more conservative learning


max_depth
Maximum interaction depth
More complex trees


min_child_weight
Minimum Hessian mass in a child
Fewer small, unstable leaves


subsample
Fraction of rows used per tree
More randomness and less overfitting


colsample_bytree
Fraction of features used per tree
Less dependence on a few features


lambda
L2 penalty on leaf weights
More shrinkage


alpha
L1 penalty on leaf weights
More sparse leaf weights



Important parameter interactions include:

decreasing eta generally requires increasing nrounds;
increasing max_depth usually calls for stronger node, row, or column regularization;
min_child_weight is measured in Hessian mass, so it is not identical to a fixed minimum row count; and
row and column subsampling add randomness, which can improve generalization but increases run-to-run variability.

Tune these values using grouped resampling or a validation season. Use early stopping to choose nrounds inside each candidate configuration. Do not choose parameters by repeatedly checking the final test season. Tutorial 2.7 demonstrates this procedure.

2 The final test is a future season
The models were developed using 2022 games. This tutorial evaluates them on 2023 games, which approximates the real task: predicting games that occur after model development.
All observations from a game remain in the same split. A random row split would put early states from a game in training and later states from that same game in testing, producing an unrealistically easy evaluation.
What metrics should be used to evaluate win probability models? Previously, performance has been measured using Brier score and log loss. But what about accuracy? Is prediction accuracy a reliable metric for evaluating probability models?

3 Model evaluation: Two scoring rules
A scoring rule in probability measures the accuracy of a probabilistic forecast by assigning a numerical penalty or reward based on a prediction and the actual outcome that occurs.
For a binary outcome yi∈{0,1}y_i\in\{0,1\} and probability pip_i, the Brier score is
Brier=1n∑i=1n(yi−pi)2,\text{Brier}=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}(y_i-p_i)^2,
and log loss is
Log loss=−1n∑i=1n[yilog(pi)+(1−yi)log(1−pi)].\text{Log loss}=-\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}
\left[y_i\log(p_i)+(1-y_i)\log(1-p_i)\right].
Both are minimized by honest probabilities, and log loss penalizes confident mistakes more severely. The next section explains precisely what “minimized by honest probabilities” means, why these two rules have that property, and why accuracy does not.

4 What makes a scoring rule proper
The question that decides whether a rule can be used to estimate probabilities is this. Suppose a forecaster knows the true probability q=P(Y=1)q=P(Y=1). Does reporting p=qp=q minimize the penalty the forecaster expects to pay? That expected penalty is
S‾(p,q)=qS(p,1)+(1−q)S(p,0).\bar S(p,q)=q\,S(p,1)+(1-q)\,S(p,0).
A rule is proper when q∈arg⁡min⁡pS‾(p,q)q\in\arg\min_p\bar S(p,q) for every q∈[0,1]q\in[0,1], and strictly proper when qq is the only minimizer. Strict propriety is the property that matters: it means every misreport is punished, so the forecaster’s best strategy is to state what it actually believes.

4.1 The Brier score is strictly proper
With S(p,y)=(y−p)2S(p,y)=(y-p)^2,
S‾(p,q)=q(1−p)2+(1−q)p2.\bar S(p,q)=q(1-p)^2+(1-q)p^2.
Expanding gives q−2pq+p2q-2pq+p^2, and completing the square yields an identity worth remembering:
S‾(p,q)=q(1−q)⏟irreducible+(p−q)2⏟cost of misreporting.\bar S(p,q)=\underbrace{q(1-q)}_{\text{irreducible}}
+\underbrace{(p-q)^2}_{\text{cost of misreporting}}.
The first term is the variance of a Bernoulli outcome. No forecaster can avoid it, and it does not depend on the forecast. The second term is zero exactly when p=qp=q and strictly positive otherwise. Therefore p=qp=q is the unique minimizer, and the Brier score is strictly proper.
Calculus confirms it:
∂S‾∂p=−2q(1−p)+2(1−q)p=2(p−q),∂2S‾∂p2=2>0.\frac{\partial\bar S}{\partial p}=-2q(1-p)+2(1-q)p=2(p-q),
\qquad
\frac{\partial^2\bar S}{\partial p^2}=2>0.
The derivative vanishes only at p=qp=q, and the function is convex.


4.2 Log loss is strictly proper
With S(p,y)=−[ylogp+(1−y)log(1−p)]S(p,y)=-\left[y\log p+(1-y)\log(1-p)\right],
S‾(p,q)=−[qlogp+(1−q)log(1−p)].\bar S(p,q)=-\left[q\log p+(1-q)\log(1-p)\right].
Subtract the penalty an honest forecaster pays, S‾(q,q)\bar S(q,q):
S‾(p,q)−S‾(q,q)=qlog⁡qp+(1−q)log⁡1−q1−p=DKL(q∥p),\bar S(p,q)-\bar S(q,q)
=q\log\frac{q}{p}+(1-q)\log\frac{1-q}{1-p}
=D_{\mathrm{KL}}(q\,\|\,p),
the Kullback–Leibler divergence from the true Bernoulli(q)(q) to the reported Bernoulli(p)(p). Gibbs’ inequality gives DKL(q∥p)≥0D_{\mathrm{KL}}(q\,\|\,p)\ge 0 with equality if and only if p=qp=q. Log loss is therefore strictly proper, and
S‾(p,q)=H(q)⏟entropy+DKL(q∥p)⏟cost of misreporting\bar S(p,q)=\underbrace{H(q)}_{\text{entropy}}
+\underbrace{D_{\mathrm{KL}}(q\,\|\,p)}_{\text{cost of misreporting}}
has the same “irreducible plus penalty” structure as the Brier score. The two rules differ in how steeply they punish: the Brier penalty grows quadratically in p−qp-q and is bounded by 1, while the log-loss penalty grows without bound as p→0p\rightarrow 0 with y=1y=1.


4.3 Accuracy is not a proper scoring rule
Accuracy first converts the forecast to a label and then checks the label. Using threshold tt, the forecaster predicts 1 when p≥tp\ge t, so as a loss
Sacc(p,y)=𝟏{𝟏(p≥t)≠y}.S_{\mathrm{acc}}(p,y)=\mathbf 1\left\{\mathbf 1(p\ge t)\ne y\right\}.
Taking the expectation over Y∼Bernoulli(q)Y\sim\text{Bernoulli}(q),
S‾acc(p,q)={1−q,p≥t,q,p<t.\bar S_{\mathrm{acc}}(p,q)=
\begin{cases}
1-q, & p\ge t,\\[2pt]
q, & p<t.
\end{cases}
The forecast enters only through which side of tt it falls on. The expected score is a two-valued step function of pp, not a function with a minimum at qq. Two distinct failures follow.
Failure 1: it is not strictly proper. Let t=0.5t=0.5 and q=0.70q=0.70. Every report in [0.5,1][0.5,1] earns the same expected error 1−q=0.301-q=0.30. Reporting the true value 0.70, reporting 0.51, and reporting 1.00 are exactly equally good. Accuracy cannot distinguish an honest forecaster from a maximally overconfident one, so it creates no incentive to be calibrated. An infinite set of reports ties with the truth.
Failure 2: at any threshold other than 0.50.5 it is not even proper. The expected error is smaller on the “predict 1” side whenever q>1/2q>1/2, so the accuracy-optimal report satisfies p≥tp\ge t if and only if q>1/2q>1/2. Honest reporting puts p≥tp\ge t exactly when q≥tq\ge t. These two rules agree only when t=1/2t=1/2.






ImportantThe practical consequence



A model selected or tuned on accuracy is being rewarded for pushing predictions toward 0 and 1, not for getting them right. In win probability that is exactly the wrong incentive: the number itself is the product.

5 Compare the model performance
This section reports the performance of all win-probability models on 2023 NFL season test data.
The accuracy column is reported for reference only. As the previous section proved, it is not a proper scoring rule, so it must not be used to rank these models.

  probability_metrics(
    predictions$home_win,
    predictions[[model_name]],
    model_name
  )
}) %>%
  bind_rows() %>%
  arrange(log_loss)

metric_table

  model         brier log_loss accuracy

1 nflverse      0.167    0.494    0.740
2 logistic      0.174    0.515    0.730
3 catboost      0.174    0.517    0.728
4 xgboost       0.176    0.520    0.722
5 lightgbm      0.176    0.520    0.725
6 bagging       0.177    0.525    0.725
7 random_forest 0.179    0.527    0.720
8 cart          0.184    0.548    0.723



metric_plot_data <- bind_rows(
  metric_table %>%
    transmute(model, metric = "Brier score", value = brier),
  metric_table %>%
    transmute(model, metric = "Log loss", value = log_loss)
)

ggplot(
  metric_plot_data,
  aes(x = value, y = reorder(model, value))
) +
  geom_col(fill = "#276FBF") +
  facet_wrap(~ metric, scales = "free_x") +
  labs(
    title = "Out-of-season probability performance",
    subtitle = "Lower is better",
    x = NULL,
    y = NULL
  ) +
  theme_minimal()








Three features of the model performance table above deserve discussion, and none of them is “the newest algorithm won.”
The logistic baseline is the strongest course model. It has both the lowest Brier score and the lowest log loss of the seven models built in this lecture. Five tutorials of tree ensembles did not beat a generalized linear model with one interaction term. That is a real and common result, not a mistake in the tutorials. The predictors are few, mostly continuous, and related to the outcome in a smooth and close-to-monotone way — score difference and time remaining behave almost exactly as a linear log-odds model assumes. Tree ensembles earn their keep when there are many predictors, sharp thresholds, high-order interactions, or categorical variables with many levels. This problem has none of those in abundance.
The lesson is the one stated in the lecture overview: a complex model must be justified against a baseline on held-out data, and here the justification fails. Reporting that honestly is the analysis. Choosing the boosted model anyway, because it is more impressive, is not.
The published nflverse model beats everything. It is trained on many more seasons, uses a richer state representation, and has been refined over years. It sets a realistic ceiling for what these eight predictors and one development season can achieve, and it shows how much of the remaining gap is data and feature engineering rather than algorithm choice.
The differences among the course models are small. The seven models span roughly .03 in log loss on 8,358 states from 272 games. Before declaring a winner, ask whether that gap is larger than the uncertainty. A bootstrap that resamples whole games, not individual states, is the right tool; Tutorial 3.6 uses the same idea for soccer shots.

set.seed(431)
game_ids <- unique(predictions$game_id)

bootstrap_gap <- replicate(400, {
  resampled_games <- sample(game_ids, length(game_ids), replace = TRUE)
  rows <- unlist(lapply(resampled_games, function(g) {
    which(predictions$game_id == g)
  }))
  log_loss(predictions$home_win[rows], predictions$xgboost[rows]) -
    log_loss(predictions$home_win[rows], predictions$logistic[rows])
})

tibble::tibble(
  comparison = "XGBoost minus logistic (log loss)",
  point_estimate = log_loss(predictions$home_win, predictions$xgboost) -
    log_loss(predictions$home_win, predictions$logistic),
  lower_95 = quantile(bootstrap_gap, 0.025),
  upper_95 = quantile(bootstrap_gap, 0.975),
  probability_xgboost_better = mean(bootstrap_gap < 0)
)

A model is calibrated if states assigned a probability near 0.70 result in a home win about 70% of the time. A calibration plot compares average predicted probability with observed win frequency.

text:
7 Repairing a miscalibrated model
When calibration fails, it is often fixable after training, without refitting the model. Two standard maps from a raw score to a calibrated probability:

Platt scaling fits a one-variable logistic regression of the outcome on the raw log odds, P(Y=1)=σ(a+blogit(p̂))P(Y=1)=\sigma(a+b\,\text{logit}(\hat p)). Two parameters, so it is stable on modest data, but it can only apply a smooth monotone correction.
Isotonic regression fits the best non-decreasing step function. It is far more flexible and can correct any monotone distortion, but it needs more data and can overfit into a staircase.

The recalibration map must be fitted on data not used to evaluate it, otherwise the improvement is an illusion. Here we split the 2023 test season in half by game: fit the maps on one half, evaluate on the other.

set.seed(431)
test_games <- unique(predictions$game_id)
fitting_games <- sample(test_games, floor(length(test_games) / 2))

fitting_half <- predictions %>% filter(game_id %in% fitting_games)
evaluation_half <- predictions %>% filter(!game_id %in% fitting_games)


logit <- function(p) {
  p <- pmin(pmax(p, 1e-6), 1 - 1e-6)
  log(p / (1 - p))
}

inverse_logit <- function(z) 1 / (1 + exp(-z))

area_under_curve <- function(truth, probability) {
  positive <- truth == 1
  ranks <- rank(probability, ties.method = "average")
  (sum(ranks[positive]) - sum(positive) * (sum(positive) + 1) / 2) /
    (sum(positive) * sum(!positive))
}

recalibrate <- function(label, fitting_probability, evaluation_probability) {
  platt <- glm(
    y ~ z,
    data = data.frame(y = fitting_half$home_win, z = logit(fitting_probability)),
    family = binomial()
  )
  platt_probability <- as.numeric(predict(
    platt,
    newdata = data.frame(z = logit(evaluation_probability)),
    type = "response"
  ))

  isotonic <- as.stepfun(isoreg(fitting_probability, fitting_half$home_win))
  isotonic_probability <- pmin(pmax(isotonic(evaluation_probability), 1e-6), 1 - 1e-6)

  truth <- evaluation_half$home_win
  tibble::tibble(
    forecast = label,
    map = c("none", "Platt", "isotonic"),
    brier = c(
      brier_score(truth, evaluation_probability),
      brier_score(truth, platt_probability),
      brier_score(truth, isotonic_probability)
    ),
    log_loss = c(
      log_loss(truth, evaluation_probability),
      log_loss(truth, platt_probability),
      log_loss(truth, isotonic_probability)
    ),
    auc = c(
      area_under_curve(truth, evaluation_probability),
      area_under_curve(truth, platt_probability),
      area_under_curve(truth, isotonic_probability)
    )
  )
}

sharpen <- function(p) inverse_logit(2.5 * logit(p))

bind_rows(
  recalibrate(
    "logistic (already calibrated)",
    fitting_half$logistic,
    evaluation_half$logistic
  ),
  recalibrate(
    "logistic, sharpened",
    sharpen(fitting_half$logistic),
    sharpen(evaluation_half$logistic)
  )
)

# A tibble: 6 × 5
  forecast                      map      brier log_loss   auc
  <chr>                         <chr>    <dbl>    <dbl> <dbl>
1 logistic (already calibrated) none     0.181    0.532 0.809
2 logistic (already calibrated) Platt    0.185    0.549 0.809
3 logistic (already calibrated) isotonic 0.187    0.595 0.806
4 logistic, sharpened           none     0.193    0.603 0.809
5 logistic, sharpened           Platt    0.185    0.549 0.809
6 logistic, sharpened           isotonic 0.187    0.595 0.806


Recalibration repairs a broken model. Sharpening drove log loss from .532 to .603; Platt scaling brings it back to .549, recovering nearly all of the damage. The fitted slope is close to 1/2.51/2.5 of the calibrated slope — the map has effectively inverted the distortion.
Recalibration does not improve an already-calibrated model; it costs you. Applied to the untouched logistic forecast, Platt scaling makes log loss slightly worse, because it spends two parameters estimated from finite data to correct a problem that was not there. Isotonic is worse still, having spent far more flexibility on noise. Recalibrate when a calibration plot shows a problem, not by reflex.






Note



Isotonic regression depends only on the order of the fitting predictions, so its results are unchanged by any monotone distortion of the input. That is why the isotonic rows are identical for the original and sharpened forecasts.

9 Inspect one game trajectory
An aggregate score can hide unreasonable jumps. A useful model should react to scores, turnovers, clock changes, and possession without producing unexplained volatility.

example_game <- predictions %>%
  count(game_id, sort = TRUE) %>%
  slice_head(n = 1) %>%
  pull(game_id)

trajectory_models <- c(
  "logistic",
  "cart",
  "random_forest",
  "xgboost",
  "lightgbm",
  "catboost"
)

trajectory_data <- lapply(trajectory_models, function(model_name) {
  predictions %>%
    filter(game_id == example_game) %>%
    transmute(
      minutes_remaining = game_seconds_remaining / 60,
      model = model_name,
      probability = .data[[model_name]]
    )

  trajectory_data,
  aes(x = minutes_remaining, y = probability, color = model)
) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) +
  scale_x_reverse() +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 1)) +

A model predicts 0.90 for two home teams. One wins and one loses. What is the two-state Brier score?
Why does log loss react more strongly than accuracy to a confident mistake?

Name two important topics that are not themselves learning algorithms but are necessary for a useful in-game model.

The threshold is t=0.70t=0.70 and the truth is q=0.60q=0.60. Find a report that beats the honest one on expected accuracy, and state why this cannot happen with a proper rule.







TipShow answers






{(1−0.90)2+(0−0.90)2}/2=(0.01+0.81)/2=0.41\{(1-0.90)^2+(0-0.90)^2\}/2=(0.01+0.81)/2=0.41.
Accuracy records only whether the probability crosses a threshold. Log loss uses the full probability and assigns a large penalty when the model gives very low probability to what actually occurs.
Overconfident. The predicted home win probability is higher than the observed rate.
It preserves the time ordering of model development and tests whether the model generalizes to games from a later period. A row split can also leak information across states from the same game.
Examples include calibration, uncertainty, data leakage prevention, monitoring, latency, failure handling, and interpretation.
q(1−q)=0.60(0.40)=0.24q(1-q)=0.60(0.40)=0.24 and (p−q)2=(0.30)2=0.09(p-q)^2=(0.30)^2=0.09, so the expected Brier score is 0.330.33. The irreducible part is 0.240.24, or about 73% of the total; only the remaining 0.090.09 is under the forecaster’s control.
Both reports are at or above the threshold, so both predict a home win and are correct with probability q=0.55q=0.55. The expected error is 0.450.45 in each case. Accuracy therefore cannot distinguish a calibrated 0.55 from a claim of certainty, so it provides no evidence about probability quality and must not be used to select the model.
Any report at or above 0.70 works, for example p=0.80p=0.80. The honest report p=0.60p=0.60 falls below t=0.70t=0.70, so it predicts “no home win” and is wrong with probability q=0.60q=0.60. Reporting p=0.80p=0.80 crosses the threshold, predicts a home win, and is wrong with probability 1−q=0.401-q=0.40. Misreporting cuts the expected error from 0.60 to 0.40. This is the general pattern: whenever q>1/2q>1/2 but q<tq<t, honesty puts the forecast on the wrong side of the threshold. A proper rule cannot be exploited this way because its expected score has a unique minimum at p=qp=q, rather than depending only on which side of a threshold pp falls.

12 Key takeaways

A scoring rule is proper when honest reporting minimizes the expected score, and strictly proper when honesty is the only minimizer.
The Brier score decomposes as q(1−q)+(p−q)2q(1-q)+(p-q)^2 and log loss as H(q)+DKL(q∥p)H(q)+D_{\mathrm{KL}}(q\|p); both are strictly proper.
Accuracy depends on the forecast only through which side of the threshold it falls on. It is not strictly proper at t=0.5t=0.5 and not proper at all for teq0.5t
eq0.5.
Never select, tune, or rank a probability model on accuracy.
Calibration asks whether a stated 70% is really 70%. It is orthogonal to ranking: AUC cannot see a calibration failure at all.
Recalibration (Platt, isotonic) repairs a miscalibrated model but must be fitted on data not used to evaluate it, and it helps nothing when calibration is already sound.
Check calibration in the segment where the model will be used, not only season-wide.
Compare models on a future season, check calibration, and confirm that a gap is larger than its bootstrap uncertainty before declaring a winner.
A complex model must beat the baseline to justify itself. In this lecture it does not, and reporting that is the analysis.
